fix(approvals): let a held card name the guard that stopped it

autoVerdict already separates destructive-guard from sensitive-guard, and
index.ts already hands that source to approvalHeldReason. The function then
branched only on native-approval and requiresExplicitApproval, so everything
else fell through to one mode-level sentence: a read-only `cat .env` and an
`rm -rf` produced byte-identical text.

The two guards exist because they are different risks. Collapsing them into
one message costs the card the only thing it knows that the user does not,
and a safe read presented as indistinguishable from a destructive one is how
people learn to stop reading approval cards at all.

local-computer-block reaches a card only over an always-allow grant that
would otherwise have fired, in a mode where nothing else speaks — so it said
nothing at all. "I pressed Always allow and it asked anyway" is a question
worth answering.

No guard changes. autoVerdict is untouched and blocks exactly what it blocked
before; only the wording of an already-held card moves.

Precedence is deliberate. Native and sandbox notes stay ahead of the guards,
and the unattended note stays ahead of them too: a fleet operator reading
"this looks destructive" would infer the next action might pass, which is the
inference #809 was written to prevent. Naming the guard is for turns a person
started.

no-grant keeps the generic note. It cannot occur in Approve-for-me at all —
an unguarded action always takes the auto grant — and in Ask or Custom the
card carries no mode explanation to begin with.

docs(store): describe what a held card actually carries

The field comment still said "destructive-looking command" from when that
was the only thing that held a card. It now carries the sensitive and
local-computer guards, the sandbox and native notes, and the free-text
error a routine or profile request failed with.

fix(i18n): translate the note on a held approval card

Every other line of an approval card goes through the catalog — the title,
the tool label, the status. The one line explaining why the bot stopped did
not, because the server composes it and the client prints it verbatim. In a
fully translated pack that is the single English sentence in the card, and it
is the sentence that matters most: it is the last thing between a bot and
someone's filesystem.

The text alone cannot move to the client, because `held` is not always copy.
Routine and profile requests put their apply error in the same field, and
that is free text with no catalog key. Cards are persisted, so text written
before any of this existed has to keep rendering too.

So the note travels as both: `heldCode` names the catalog key, `held` keeps
the English. The client translates by key and falls back to the text, which
covers an older card, an apply error, and a client meeting a server that
knows a key it does not.

The branching that picks the note stays in one place. approvalHeldNote
returns the key, approvalHeldReason is that plus a lookup, so the two can
never disagree about which note a card gets. A test walks every context
combination to hold that, and pins each key's English against the shipped
catalog so the server and the pack cannot drift apart silently.

All eight packs carry the ten new notes, so German stays complete and the
other six gain their first translated approval copy. The mode labels stay in
English inside them on purpose: ApprovalModeSelector renders "Approve for me"
and "Full access" without t(), so a translated note would name a button the
reader cannot find. "Always allow" is in the catalog, so that one is
translated and matches its button. A test pins both halves of that rule.

A paired device's session used to end exactly 30 days after pairing, however
often it was used. Now a session used past its halfway mark is renewed for
the full term, the browser's cookie is re-issued once per renewal so it
does not lapse before the server's record, and OMB_SESSION_TTL_DAYS changes
the term. A session that goes quiet still expires; nothing expired is revived.

Review points from a second pass: a 403 must not extend a session; a
renewal without an absolute cap makes a stolen cookie immortal; sending
the refreshed cookie exactly once loses it on a dropped response or a
restart; env values need bounds; four docs still described the old rule.

term the cap forbids; redeeming a stream ticket is not use of the session;
the docs still said 15 days where the rule is half the term; an old
sessions.json meets the cap without losing the term it has; the cookie

ux(desktop): put reasoning effort beside the model picker (#880)

Effort only existed inside the per-bot settings dialog, while the model it
qualifies is chosen from the conversation header. People pick a model and its
effort as one decision, so the control was easy to miss where it lived.

The levels now live in an EffortRow that the picker's popover and the settings
dialog both render, writing through the same setModel dispatch. Sharing one
component is what keeps the two surfaces from drifting: previously the dialog
patched the bot record while the picker dispatched setModel, two paths to the
same field. The row reads the levels off the engine the bot actually runs on,
so an engine that declares none renders nothing rather than an empty control,
and a level the server would reject is never offered.

Default stays distinct from the `none` level: Default sends no level and lets
the engine decide, `none` is a level the engine is told to use. Only pi offers
both, and collapsing them would change what already-configured bots send.

* feat(rooms): show when a bot answers from a private thread

#754 gave bots recall, and it rides in room turns: a bot mentioned in a
channel can answer about work discussed in its DM. That is the feature.
The gap is disclosure — when it happens, nobody in the room can see it.

Announce the crossing where it lands. When session_search or session_read
returns a hit from a thread that is not the current one, and the current
thread is a room, append an activity chip: "<Bot> recalled 2 messages from
its private chat with you". It reuses the chip room turns already use for
"finishing another conversation".

- once per (room, source thread), so a bot that searches three times in a
  turn leaves one chip per private thread rather than one per search
- the ledger is in memory, so a restart re-announces: a duplicate chip is
  noise, a missing one is the whole bug
- a 1:1 stays silent — there is nothing to disclose when the user already
  owns every thread the bot can reach

The model is told too. Crossed hits are marked `private to this user` in
the tool output, with a closing line saying the room has been shown the
recall and it should say where something came from if asked. Without that
the bot cannot answer "where did you get that?" honestly.

Not included: the first-disclosure confirmation from the issue. That needs
persisted per-room consent and a card flow, and the visible half is worth
shipping before the asking half.

Refs #776

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(browser): picture the page a bot browsed, not nothing and not its desktop

A bot opens a page, the tools run, the bot describes it correctly — and the
transcript settles with no picture. The Browser panel meanwhile promises
"pages the bot looks at appear in the chat as screenshots".

Two causes, both left by the engine swap.

The screen gate still lists the Electron surface's tool names. agent-browser
calls its tools agent_browser_open / _click / _screenshot, none of which
match, so `touched` never flips and every browser turn settles as if the bot
had never looked at a screen.

And nothing supplies a browser frame any more. `startScreenPoller` runs only
when `previewCapture` is set, and that is assigned solely by the computer
branches; the browser's capture lived in the deleted browser-proxy.ts and was
never replaced. A browser-only bot has no frame source at all.

Fixing only the first would be worse than the bug for a bot holding both
surfaces: agent-browser runs its own headless Chrome on the host, not inside
the bot's desktop, so a web-browsing turn would settle with a picture of an
idle Local VM. The interface would be confidently showing the wrong room.

So the poller now holds both captures and pictures whichever surface the
touching tool acted on — a browser tool the page, a computer tool the
desktop, and a status read redirects nothing.

- agentBrowserFrame() runs the pinned binary with the same session env as the
  MCP mount, so it photographs the daemon the bot is already driving rather
  than starting a second browser beside it
- a 10s cap: a hung browser must not hold the fold open, and a missing
  picture beats a stuck turn
- read-only browser tools stay out of the gate by the rule already applied
  everywhere else in that list — snapshot, read and get_text return text, and
  the waits change nothing the action before them did not already count

Closes #906

perf(sse): stop buffering screen frames for a client that can't drain

broadcast() wrote every frame with `client.res.write(frame)` and threw the
boolean return away, so a slow or stalled remote client had every subsequent
frame queued in Node's per-connection write buffer with nothing ever
consulting backpressure. Screen captures are the exposed path: hundreds of
kilobytes each, broadcast through the same fan-out, and on by default.

deliverSseFrame() now makes one decision per client per frame:

  - over 4 MB buffered, end the connection. Its EventSource reconnects and
    replays through the existing Last-Event-ID/replayBuffer path, so nothing
    is silently lost.
  - backpressured and the frame is a screen capture, drop it. The next
    capture supersedes whatever was dropped.
  - otherwise write it. Durable events are never dropped on the backpressure
    flag alone.

The flag clears on the socket's `drain` event, and that matters more than it
looks: write() returns false as soon as buffered bytes pass the socket's 16 KB
highWaterMark, which a single screen frame clears on its own. Without the
drain listener the flag latches for the life of the connection and a perfectly
healthy client stops receiving screen frames after its first one. One listener
per episode, not per frame.

It lives in its own file rather than inside index.ts because index.ts calls
server.listen() as an import-time side effect — that is why the existing SSE
coverage in index.test.ts spawns a subprocess instead of importing. A
dependency-free function can be driven with a fake response object directly.

Verified: 7 unit cases in server/sse-fanout.test.ts covering normal send, the
flag on write()===false, screen dropped while a durable event is not,
resumption after drain, one listener per episode, disconnect over the byte
bound, and a throwing write(). server/index.test.ts full file 198 passed /
1 skipped, including "resumable event stream" and "computer control API".
pnpm typecheck clean.

Not verified: no test drives a real throttled TCP consumer, so real-socket
writableLength growth is modelled by a standalone simulation of this function
rather than measured against the live server. That simulation, 500 frames of
200 KB to a never-draining socket, held writableLength at 0.195 MB against
97.7 MB before the change.

perf(attachments): account committed bytes instead of rescanning per MiB

The attachment quota check walked the whole attachments directory with
readdirSync + statSync, and it ran inside AttachmentReservation.reserveAtLeast
— which fires once per ~1 MiB chunk for an unknown-length streamed upload. A
25 MiB upload did ~25 full scans, each proportional to how many files were
already there, all synchronous on the shared event loop. An authenticated
client could degrade the server for everyone just by uploading.

Committed bytes are now cached: one scan from cold per process, then O(1)
updates on commit and delete. Reservation reads the cache instead of the disk.
Two more scans went away with it — the UUID-collision check stats the handful
of extensions saveFile/saveImage can produce rather than listing the
directory, and stale-partial cleanup left the per-chunk path.

Measured on an isolated fixture, 25 MiB unknown-length upload, before → after:

  existing files    total time         max event-loop delay
  0                 40 ms  →  36 ms    0 ms  →  0 ms
  1,000            511 ms  →  55 ms   14 ms  →  0 ms
  5,000          5,510 ms  →  67 ms  332 ms  →  0 ms

Flat instead of scaling with directory size. The delay column is the one that
matters: 332 ms of blocked loop meant every other request waited on one
client's upload.

Correctness, since this is a quota path and overcounting rejects uploads that
should fit while undercounting lets a client past the limit:

  - cold start scans real disk state before trusting anything, so a process
    that boots onto a directory full of files gets the right total;
  - every delete of a committed attachment routes through the new
    deleteAttachment(), including the three raw unlinkSync call sites in
    index.ts (thread image purge, retired provider turn, avatar rollback), so
    a delete can never leave the cache high;
  - reservation still happens before any byte is written, so the cache is
    never read mid-write of the file it is about to account for;
  - abandoned uploads never touch the cache — only a successful link adds to
    it — and every decrement clamps at 0, so drift degrades to a stale-low
    number the next scan corrects, not a negative.

Moving cleanup out of the hot path removed its only caller, which would have
let a crash-orphaned partial hold quota forever, so the server sweeps once at
start-up and warms the cache off that same scan.

Known limit, unchanged in kind: the cache is single-process and will not see
another process writing to the same attachments directory. uploadLocks already
assumes one server per data dir.

server/attachments.test.ts: 24 passed, including new cases for delete
accounting, a fresh process against pre-existing files, and the explicit
cleanup sweep. server/index.test.ts: 198 passed, 1 skipped. pnpm typecheck
clean.

fix(electron): prove a data-directory lease dead across a reboot (#937)

* fix(electron): prove a data-directory lease dead across a reboot

A pid does not identify a process across a restart. The kernel restarts
pid allocation, so the low pid a login-item launch records is routinely
reused by a root-owned daemon on the next boot; process.kill(pid, 0)
then answers EPERM, which the lease reads as "alive". The desktop showed
"already using this data directory (process 459). Close the other
instance first." on every launch, with no instance for anyone to close
and no in-app recovery -- a permanent brick after one unclean shutdown.

Record which boot wrote the lease and require a match before believing
the owner is alive. The pid check is unchanged and still required; boot
identity can only ever prove a record DEAD, never alive, because a wrong
"stale" verdict would let two instances share one data directory -- the
exact harm this module exists to prevent. Both signals are exact rather
than heuristic, and neither is derived from the wall clock, which NTP
can move:

  - darwin/linux: the kernel's boot session id, fixed for one boot.
  - elsewhere (Windows has no equivalent): a since-boot clock cannot run
    backwards within a boot, so a recorded uptime above the machine's
    current uptime can only have been written before a reboot.

Records written by older builds carry neither field and keep the
previous pid-only behaviour exactly, so an in-place upgrade cannot fail
on an "invalid lease".

The contention message now names the lease record, so anyone still stuck
-- a Windows reboot the uptime check cannot prove -- can recover without
support.

fix(chat): resolve message direction per block so RTL content renders correctly (#994)

* fix(chat): resolve message direction per block so RTL content renders correctly

Message text is written in the user's or the model's language, which is
independent of the UI language. Every block in a bubble inherited the app's
LTR, so an Arabic or Hebrew answer came out left-aligned with its punctuation
displaced, its list markers and blockquote rule on the wrong side, and its
table columns in the wrong order.

Each block now resolves its own direction from its own first strong character,
and the physical box properties around message content become logical ones
(pl-5 → ps-5, border-l-2 → border-s-2, text-left → text-start).

Direction is computed here rather than delegated to HTML's dir="auto": that
algorithm ignores any descendant carrying its own dir, so a blockquote whose
paragraphs each resolved their own direction found no text left to judge and
fell back to LTR — and a table whose cells resolved individually never
reversed its columns. Tables and lists resolve once at the container so cells
and markers stay aligned with the indent that makes room for them.

Code is the exception and pins dir="ltr": fenced blocks, inline spans, links
and local file paths isolate themselves, so a snippet never reorders and never
scrambles the RTL sentence holding it. Code is also skipped when judging a
block, so an answer opening with `fs.readFileSync` and continuing in Arabic is
still an Arabic paragraph.

Plain-text bodies (user turns, webhook tasks, error fallbacks) use
unicode-bidi: plaintext, which resolves per line — a pasted block mixing an
Arabic sentence with an English stack trace lays each line out on its own
instead of letting the first decide for all of them. The composer carries
dir="auto" so a message reads the same while it is typed as after it is sent.

The app's own chrome is untouched: this is content direction, not UI locale.

paragraph, sends a user turn whose lines alternate script, and mounts the real
renderer against its own disposable home.

Android: opt-in background connection so scheduled reminders survive the app being closed (#966)

* Android: keep the companion connected in the background, on request

Adds an opt-in "Background connection" toggle (Settings, off by
default) that runs a real foreground service to hold the SSE stream
open indefinitely, instead of only the existing 25-second post-
background linger window. Without this, a scheduled routine/reminder
that fires while the app is fully closed never reaches the phone --
LocalNotificationPoster only ever delivers "live/replayed" frames,
and the linger window (SessionLingerService, deliberately not a
foreground service) only buys ~25s after backgrounding.

- AlwaysOnConnectionService: foregroundServiceType="connectedDevice"
  (not "dataSync", which faces a 6h/24h cap on Android 15+),
  stopWithTask="false" so it survives the app being swiped away,
  START_STICKY so the OS restarts it if killed under pressure.
- AlwaysOnConnectionState: a main-thread-confined flag
  SessionLingerController.onStop() checks to skip its own 25s window
  when the service is already holding the process open -- the two
  mechanisms coordinate rather than race each other.
- AlwaysOnBootReceiver: restarts the service after a reboot if the
  user left it enabled; OpenMausApp.onCreate() covers the "process
  relaunched, not rebooted" case the same way.
- Battery-optimization exemption is requested once, only when turning
  the toggle on (MainActivity.requestIgnoreBatteryOptimizations).
- Settings toggle wired through CompanionEnvironment the same way
  every other permission/preference control already is.

Also bumps the "done" notification channel (bot replies / finished
tasks) from DEFAULT to HIGH importance so it pops up with sound
rather than landing silently in the shade -- channel importance can
only be set at first creation on a given device, so this ships as a
new channel id ("bot_messages") with the old "done" channel deleted
on upgrade, rather than trying to reconfigure the existing one in
place.

SessionLingerWiringTest's manifest-wide "never contains
FOREGROUND_SERVICE" assertion is narrowed to the per-element checks
it already had on SessionLingerService specifically: that was always
a proxy for "the linger *service* doesn't need one", not a ban on the
app ever using FOREGROUND_SERVICE for a different, user-opted-in job.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf(claude): stop a memory edit from re-uploading the whole session

The Claude driver keeps one CLI process per thread and keys it on the
spawn contract, which includes the system prompt. MEMORY.md is pasted
into that prompt, so the moment a bot saved a memory the contract
changed, the process relaunched, and the provider re-cached the entire
conversation at the cache-write rate. Mentions did the same on any turn
that tagged a bot. In the measured thread two of the six full re-uploads
were this, ~400k written tokens.

Split the prompt at the sections that legitimately differ between two
turns of one live conversation — memory and mentions — and report the
halves separately (`systemStable`, `systemVolatile`). The driver keys
its process on the stable half only. A fresh process still gets the whole
prompt; a live one is told what changed inside the next turn, in the
CLI's own out-of-band form, which costs a short append instead of a
relaunch.

`system` is unchanged, so every other driver keeps reading exactly what
it read before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(mcp): trim an oversized tool result before it reaches the model

One tool call can put more into a conversation than everything else in
it. A single Instamart product search returns 60-140 KB of JSON and a
restaurant menu 70-105 KB; four searches in one turn added 67k tokens to
a food-ordering thread, and every later model call in that session
re-read all of it. That thread ended at 330k tokens per call.

On a vendor-CLI engine the harness never sees these calls — the CLI runs
the server itself and appends the raw answer to the session it owns — so
the only place to stand is between the two processes. mcp-gate.ts is a
pass-through MCP server: every frame is relayed untouched except the
response to a tools/call, where an oversized result is cut to a budget,
the untrimmed text is written to a file under the data dir, and the
model is told in the result where that file is so it can read or grep
the rest with its ordinary tools. Nothing is lost.

The cut keeps whole records: the payload is parsed and its bulk arrays
truncated, so a model is never handed half an object, and structured
content is trimmed the same way rather than left as a full second copy.
A payload that is not JSON falls back to a text cut that says so. A
result the trimmer cannot handle is relayed whole — costing context is
recoverable, dropping a tool's answer is not.

Only bot-owned servers are gated (the app's custom servers and the bot
project's .mcp.json). Harness-owned mounts — the permission broker,
computer, browser, agents, dweb — are already bounded and stay direct.
An http/sse entry has no process to stand between and is mounted as it
was.

OMB_MCP_RESULT_BUDGET sets the budget; 0 mounts bot servers directly.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf(claude): compact the CLI session at a window the harness picks

The CLI compacts when it nears a window, and left alone that window is
the model's own. A Sonnet 5 session therefore runs toward a million
tokens before anything happens, and every model call until then re-reads
the whole session. The measured thread sat at 330k tokens per call and
looked perfectly healthy to the CLI.

Pass --autocompact so the harness chooses the window (200k by default),
delegating the compaction itself to the CLI, which owns the session and
already has a summarizer for it. With bot tool results gated most threads
never reach the window; this is the backstop for the ones that do.

OMB_CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT takes a token count, "auto" to hand the decision
back to the CLI, or "off" to pass nothing. A configured value is clamped
to the 100k-1M the CLI accepts, because out of range is an argument error
that would fail every turn rather than degrade.

fix(claude): recover a thread whose resume never answers (#1038)

A --resume the CLI never acknowledged bricked the thread: the CLI exited
before its `init` frame, the failure was terminal so nothing retried, and the
dead cursor was never cleared — so every later turn resumed the same missing
session and failed identically, with no way back except switching engines.

The driver now classifies the failure from its own protocol state
(server/resume-recovery.ts): a resume was offered, no `init` arrived, nothing
streamed. Only that "before-accept" case is replayed, exactly once, on a
fresh session; a session that emitted `init` and then died may already have
run tools, so it is reported like any other failure. Error text is never
consulted — provider strings are prose that gets reworded and localized.

The fresh session is not blank: the harness attaches SendTurnInput.recoveryText
alongside every resumeCursor — the active branch replayed inline
(turn-context.ts buildRecoveryText) — and that is what the recovered turn
carries. The harness records the new session's cursor from `session.started`
as it always did.

Lifted from #759 (aivsomkar), adapted to main: the rebuild came from that
branch's context plan; here it is the recovery text.

Tests: refused resume recovers with the rebuild on a fresh launch and emits
turn.retrying(resume_rejected); a launch that fails every time settles as
failed after one relaunch; a resumed session that emitted init then died is
never resent; a crash on a launch that offered no cursor is never treated as
a refused resume; a fresh turn never rebuilds; classification and prompt
selection; buildRecoveryText. Mutation-checked: sending the bare text instead
of the rebuild, treating every failure as a refused resume, and never
recording init each fail a test.

security(electron): guard open-external origin and restrict session permissions (#986)

* security(electron): guard open-external origin and restrict session permissions

Harden Electron application boundaries against unprivileged IPC calls and excessive permission grants:

1. desktop:open-external IPC handler:
   Wrap with localOnly(...) to enforce the two-wall defense-in-depth model, ensuring remote or unprivileged frames cannot invoke host external browser launches. Additionally reject URLs carrying credentials in user info (url.username || url.password).

2. session.defaultSession permissions:
   Replace the permissive origin-only check with an explicit permission policy (appPermissionAllowed), matching the pattern established in desktop-viewer-permissions.mjs. Allow only safe UI capabilities (notifications, clipboard, fullscreen) and audio-only media (microphone), while explicitly denying privileged and unneeded Chromium APIs (camera/video, geolocation, USB, MIDI, serial, HID).

Tested:
- electron/app-permissions.node-test.mjs: grants notifications/clipboard/fullscreen/mic, denies camera/video and privileged capabilities, rejects cross-origin and opaque requests.
- electron/local-origin.node-test.mjs: verifies desktop:open-external is protected by localOnly.
- electron/local-only-hoist.node-test.mjs: verifies binding order against module-level crashes.

fix(approvals): Auto answers itself when Claude's reviewer never starts (#1088)

"Approve for me" hands every permission to the provider's own reviewer and
never second-guesses it. Claude Code accepts `--permission-mode auto` for any
model and, when auto mode is unavailable (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5 on 2.1.266,
or an org that disabled it), silently starts in Manual, so every tool call
reached the harness as a "reviewer's verdict" and carded the person for
`wc -l` in the bot's own workspace.

The Claude driver now reads the effective permission mode from the CLI's
init frame and tags each request.opened with nativeReview "active" or
"inactive". When Auto was requested and the session runs Manual, autoVerdict
falls back to safe Auto: routine actions approve (logged with rule
native-review-inactive), the destructive/sensitive guards, unattended turns
and host control still card, and the chat gets one notice per session naming
the model. A request from a reviewer known to be running is still never
answered by the app.

For reviewers nobody can observe (Grok's is feature-gated, Codex's asks are
its own), an "Always allow" the person recorded for that exact key now
answers the next identical punt, and the card offers to remember it. Auto's
blanket approval does not apply there, so a reviewer that did block
something is never overruled by a regex.

fix: answer AskUserQuestion with the model's own options, not Allow/Deny (#953)

* fix: answer AskUserQuestion with the model's own options, not Allow/Deny

Claude's built-in AskUserQuestion reaches OpenMausBot as a permission ask —
the CLI routes it through --permission-prompt-tool like any other tool use.
So a question like "which model should this bot run on?" arrived as a card
offering Deny / Always allow / Allow once, and answering it "allow" made the
CLI run the tool against an interface that isn't there: the result came back
"The user did not answer the questions" and the answer was dropped.

The permission proxy now recognises that one tool and forwards it as a
QUESTION carrying the model's structured questions. The desktop draws them
as a card — a tab per question, the model's own options with their
descriptions, an "Other" free-text row, one submit — and the answer goes
back on the deny channel, which is the only branch whose message the CLI
hands to the model verbatim as the tool result. Verified end to end against
claude 2.1.260.

Also here, because the same gap made them wrong:
- No approval mode may auto-answer a structured ask, whatever channel the
  provider routed it through.
- An answered question keeps its words (`answeredText`), so a settled card
  still shows what was chosen after a reload instead of "answer".
- Single-question asks also send flat option labels, so the iOS and Android
  companions can answer them with the buttons they already draw.

* Show clickable options when a bot asks you a question

The Claude CLI has its own AskUserQuestion tool for asking the user to
pick from a list. It reached us through the permission tool, so we
treated it as "may I run this?" and drew an Allow/Deny box over a
truncated blob of JSON. The buttons the bot meant you to press were
never shown, and auto mode could answer the question for you.

It is now read as what it is: a question. Each one becomes a normal
option card with real buttons and each option's own explanation, and the
answer goes back in the field the tool documents for it. A bare allow is
not enough — the CLI then runs the tool in a headless session with no
dialog and tells the model you did not answer, so the click is thrown
away. Verified end to end against claude 2.1.238.

  refuses a denial on a question, so closing one used to do nothing.

fix(atomic): retry a rename Windows refuses for a moment (#1097)

Closes #9. Windows refuses a rename onto an existing path while anything else
holds a handle to either file, and a virus scanner or the search indexer
opening a just-closed file for a few milliseconds is enough. It surfaced as
EPERM from `renameSync` in `writeFileAtomic`, and every caller treats a throw
there as a failed save — so `Store.saveBots`, `RoutineManager.save` and staged
skill writes lost the write. Through an HTTP handler it did not even look like
a filesystem error: `POST /api/teams/import` returned 500.

EPERM, EACCES and EBUSY are now retried with a fixed backoff — 5, 10, 20, 40,
80 ms, six attempts, ~155 ms worst case. Every other code still throws on the
first attempt: busy-waiting on a missing directory or a cross-device rename
would hide a real bug behind a delay and fail anyway.

Kept synchronous. Every caller is a synchronous save path, and making one of
them async is a far larger change than this warrants.

`renameWithRetry` takes an injectable `rename` because there is no portable way
to make a real filesystem produce a transient EPERM on demand.

Verified: server/atomic.test.ts 9 passed, 1 skipped — the 7 existing cases plus
4 new ones covering a transient EPERM succeeding, EACCES/EBUSY treated the
same, giving up after six attempts, and ENOENT/EXDEV/EISDIR not being retried
at all. The three suites that produced these failures all session —
team-backup, routine-requests and skills — now pass 92/92 together.

One side effect worth knowing: replacing a file with a directory raises
EPERM/EACCES on some platforms, so that failure now takes ~155 ms before
throwing. The existing "cleans up the temporary file when replacement fails"
test still passes; it is slower, not wrong.

fix(permission-broker): scope broker socket by bot id, not threadId alone (#1102)

* fix(permission-broker): scope broker socket by bot id, not threadId alone

The Claude driver's session/permission-broker resource table is a single
process-wide map keyed only on threadId. When a delegated child turn's
threadId ever coincides with its still-open parent's — as reproduced
repeatedly against a live @Chief -> @Cliff delegation on Windows (#1017,
"permission broker: ... is still held") — both turns collide on the exact
same broker socket. On POSIX this gets papered over by unlinkSync stealing
the socket file out from under the still-listening parent; on Windows,
named pipes are exclusive and the collision surfaces as an outright bind
failure, breaking the delegated tool-call channel itself (not just the
approval card), even with Full access on both bots.

Fold botId into the socket-path digest so a delegated child can never
share a broker socket with its parent (or any other bot), regardless of
the exact mechanism that produces the threadId reuse.

Fixes #1017.

perf(messages): read the newest N rows in SQL instead of the whole thread (#1100)

PERF-01 from the 2026-09-07 audit. GET /api/bots called messagesFor(),
which called Store.thread(), which ran a SELECT with no LIMIT — so every
startup and every reconnect hydrated and JSON-parsed the complete transcript
of every bot and group before messagePage() sliced it down to the last N.
publicBot() then loaded the same full transcript a second time, only for
messagePage()'s spread to overwrite it. Cost scaled with lifetime history
rather than with what anyone was going to look at, worst on long threads
carrying inline screen-capture PNGs. Asking for ?messages=50 never helped:
the unbounded load already happened before the slice.

readThreadTail() reads `ORDER BY rowid DESC LIMIT n+1` at the SQL boundary
and reverses; the extra row is how hasMore is known. Store.messagesTail()
sits on top: an in-memory slice when the thread is already cached, the
bounded read when it is not, and a full load when the bounded read comes
back as the whole thread anyway (short thread, or a first-touch legacy
import) so a later messagesFor() does not re-read it.

Two correctness details the shape forces:

Legacy rows predate per-message parentId and are chained by array order on
load, which a bounded page cannot reconstruct — so a tail read that returns
any unparented row falls back to the full load rather than handing back a
broken parent chain.

Paging backwards with `before` still uses the full cached array. Seeking to
an arbitrary point in history is not what a LIMIT on the newest rows can do,
and that path is not the startup cost this fixes.

At the /api/bots call site publicBot() gives way to wireBot(), since
messagePage() already supplies messages and activeLeafId. tasks is passed
explicitly there: it is the one field publicBot() adds that messagePage()
does not, and wireBot() omits the key entirely for a bot record with no
tasks where publicBot() always sent [].

Measured on isolated synthetic threads, cold Store, ~1 message in 25
carrying a ~60 KB base64 PNG — old messagesFor()+slice(-50) against new
messagesTail(50):

  thread length    old        new       response bytes
  200              1.92 ms    0.89 ms   9,921
  1,000            5.26 ms    2.97 ms   9,921
  5,000           14.34 ms    0.82 ms   9,969
  20,000          80.25 ms    1.97 ms  10,017

Flat instead of linear, and the response bytes barely move at any size —
which is the audit's point restated: this was never bytes on the wire, it
was unbounded server work behind a slice.

Who benefits today: the Android and iOS companions already request
?messages=50 (android/core/.../ClientTest.kt asserts exactly that call) and
already implement hasImage plus on-demand image fetch, so they get the whole
win now. The desktop renderer still hydrates unbounded on purpose —
slimMessage() strips png/mime from a bounded page and ChatView renders
`m.png ? <ScreenFrame/> : null` with no fetch-on-demand and no older-page
loading, so turning the limit on today would silently vanish recent screen
captures with no way to get them back. Closing that is renderer work, with
the companions as the template.

Verified: server/message-db.test.ts and server/store.test.ts 86 passed,
including new cases for the newest-N read, hasMore both ways, the legacy
import fallback, and that a later messagesFor() on the same Store still
returns full history. pnpm typecheck clean. server/index.test.ts 197 passed
/ 1 skipped with one failure that moves between runs and passes in
isolation — this run a 500 from POST /api/teams/import, an earlier run an
unrelated SSE notification assertion. Both are consistent with the Windows
EPERM-on-renameSync flake this repo already carries (a failed atomic write
inside an import surfaces as a 500), not with anything here.

fix(threads): fold bot-closed threads out of the sidebar (#1108)

* fix(threads): fold bot-closed threads out of the sidebar

close_thread only wrote a "Closed by" chip into the transcript and cleared
unread; the task record carried no closed state, so a closed thread stayed
in the sidebar looking exactly like an open one. A PM bot that opened ten
helper threads and closed them left ten rows behind, and those rows also
spent the sidebar's six recent slots, pushing the person's own threads out.

The task now carries `closedBy` (who, when), stamped by close_thread and
cleared the moment a new turn starts there, so a thread the person picks
back up is simply open again. The sidebar folds closed threads out of the
default list without counting them against the six recent rows; "show all"
and search still list them, dimmed, with "closed by <bot>" under the title.
Nothing is deleted — deletion stays the person's confirmed action.

list_threads reports state "closed", closing twice is a quiet no-op with no
second chip, and team backups carry the stamp with the closer remapped like
the opener, so a tidied pile does not come back as a pile after import.

scripts/repro-closed-threads.mjs drives the same internal endpoints against
an isolated fake-engine server and reports whether the stamp holds.

Fixes MOCA-92.

  the same free/busy test holdWhileTargetBusy uses (targetCanTakeTurn),
  and only after dropIfUnreachable/dropIfThreadGone. A handoff whose
  target is free right now is delivered instead of expired, so time the
  app was closed or asleep no longer consumes the 24 hours (boot resets
  every bot to idle; a missed hourly-sweep tick on wake finds a target
  that may already be free). A deleted target still counts as
  unreachable, so orphaned items still expire. Same rule applied to the
  post-approval dispatch path.
- Minor: a legacy item loaded with attempts >= 1 is marked
  waitAnnounced so it doesn't post a second waiting chip.
- Minor: _loadPending clamps a future queuedAt to now and persists a
  backfilled queuedAt immediately so a restart loop can't keep resetting
  the 24-hour window.
- Minor: delegations.test.ts's waitFor uses performance.now() for its
  deadline so a regression fails at 2s instead of hanging under fake
  timers.

- check_delegation reports a deleted target as "unavailable" instead of
  falling through to peerStatus's "available" default.

  hours"; it now says the handoff is past its 24-hour limit and expires
  the next time it cannot be delivered.
- Documented three previously-unlisted spec deviations (peerStatus's
  two-argument signature, expireDelegation's ownerId-gated chip, and
  expiry's position after the reachability gates) and updated the
  design doc's expiry section to match.

expireStaleDelegations case (RED against the old code, GREEN after),

fix(windows): give this app its own daemon instead of adopting the shared one

The default pipe on Windows is shared: another agent tool, a CLI session,
or the user's own cua-driver install may already own it, possibly on a
different version or permission mode than the one this app ships. The
previous revision attached to whatever was listening there, which would
silently hand computer use to a process this app neither owns nor can
reason about, and made the driver version depend on the machine.

same endpoint to the MCP proxy. The shared pipe is only probed, and only
to log why a second daemon exists. The macOS dev path that adopts a
running CuaDriver.app is left as it was and is now gated to darwin
explicitly, so Windows can never reach it.

daemon already running: the private pipe comes up, the MCP proxy answers
on it, and the shared pipe is exactly as it was before and after.

fix(coordination): keep a minimum runway when the handoff lifetime ceiling hits

The 30-minute tree lifetime was measured from the root's createdAt for
every node on every tick, so a node that started seconds earlier was
aborted mid-run with the generic "Room request timed out" message, and a
follow-up enqueued in the root's final minutes passed the enqueue guard
only to be killed minutes later.

Each node now keeps a 10-minute minimum runway from its own execution
start (whichever of the tree ceiling and that runway is later), an
ancestor past its ceiling waits for a descendant still running inside
its runway, new work is refused when the remaining root lifetime cannot
serve the runway, and the failure message names the budget, the node
status, and elapsed time.

fix(coordination): give a resumed parent its runway past the ceiling

The expiry loop ran before the reporting loop, so a waiting parent whose children had all settled was failed at the tree ceiling before it could turn into resume; the follow-up execution that decides on the children results never ran. A node that still owes that follow-up (resume, or waiting with every child terminal, recursively) is now preserved past the ceiling, and its deadline comes from the follow-up execution start via the existing minimum runway. test(android): stop the P1-04 failover waits timing out on a slow runner

`invalidCertificateAndEveryGatewayStatusMoveOnlyToProtectedRoute` timed
out waiting 3500 ms for the session to reach the protected route. The
tree it failed on had an `android/` byte-identical to a green `main`, and
the job passed on ~30 other runs including two earlier ones on the same
branch — so this is the window being too tight, not the routing being
wrong.

Reaching the protected route after a refused authority costs a reconnect
backoff (Session doubles it 1s → 15s) plus real TLS handshakes against
three MockWebServers. 3500 ms covers that on a quiet laptop and not
always on a shared CI runner, so the test failed the run for being slow
rather than for being wrong.

`eventually()` returns the moment its condition holds, so raising the
ceiling costs a passing run nothing — it only bounds how long we wait
before calling the session hung. The assertions after each wait are
untouched and still judge the routing: a run that reaches the protected
route via a retried bad authority still fails, loudly.

Both failover waits now share one named constant so the intent reads as
"detect a hang" rather than "assert a latency".

Kotlin suite or mutation-check the change. The argument is from the code
and the CI record, and CI is what exercises it.

fix(computer): show the cloud screen while a turn is using it

Opening the Computer panel for a Cloud bot always went through
`POST /computer/provision`, because `resolveBoxPanelAction` answers an
explicit Cloud choice with "ensure-box" regardless of what the bot is
doing. The server refuses provision and sleep with 409 while a turn owns
the box, so the panel landed in the error phase: "Couldn't reach the
computer" over a red "being used by an active turn — interrupt it first".
Since the phase never reached ready, `cloudPreviewReady` stayed false, the
screenshot poll never started and the live `screen` frames the turn was
already broadcasting were ignored. The one moment a person most wants to
watch the screen was the moment the panel refused to show it.

The resolver now takes `busy`. Mid-turn, a ready box is attached as-is —
no POST, phase goes straight to ready, and the turn's live frames plus the
existing busy-cadence screenshot poll show what the bot is doing. A box
that is not ready yet is left to the turn, which creates or wakes it, and
the panel shows a neutral "your bot is using this computer right now"
state instead of an error. `bot.busy` joins the effect's dependencies so
the panel re-resolves when a turn starts or ends, and a provision that
races a starting turn and gets the 409 falls into the same waiting state.

The cloud-preview fixture refuses provision while Busy is on, like the
server, so the verification checklist gains this transition. Server code
is unchanged: screenshot and join were never gated during a turn.

A user watched the thread's usage chip grow by 200-300k tokens per message

headlined input plus output, where input counts every token the model read

whole thread, so a four-call turn on a 70k thread really is ~280k tokens, of
which nine tenths were cache. Every other usage tool headlines cost or fresh
tokens and puts that number in a column.

model had not seen before plus what it wrote, and keeps the raw total for
engines that never report a cached share. Beside it sits the context figure —
what the last model call's prompt held against the model's window — with the
thresholds ccusage uses (warning at 50%, danger at 80%) and a nudge to start a
new thread past that. The tooltip adds what the last message alone cost.

Drivers now say what filled the window: Claude per assistant message, Codex
from the last call and the window Codex reports. The Codex driver banks a
turn as the process total minus whatever the process carried in before the
server named the turn, so a resumed thread's restored usage is neither
counted again nor mistaken for this turn, and a multi-step turn is no longer
reduced to its final call. A conservative model-family table supplies the
window when the driver does not.

fix(coordination): port the snapshot probe to the version floor, and dedup on the wire spelling

Rebasing this onto main needed two substantive changes, not just conflict
resolution.

**The --help probe no longer exists.** This branch gated
`--system-prompt-snapshot` behind `claudeCliHelpSupportsFlag(cliHelp, ...)`,
but #1214 removed help-text probing from the Claude driver — `cliHelp`,
`claudeCliHelpSupportsFlag` and the fake CLI's `--help` branch are all gone
from main, which reverted a3b1d61e back to version floors. Left as written,
this branch would not typecheck, and its new tests would spawn the fake CLI
with `--help`, get no answer, and block until the 8s timeout.

Ported to main's existing mechanism instead: `--system-prompt-snapshot` is
registered in CLAUDE_FLAG_FLOORS at 2.1.267 (the first CLI that accepts it)
and gated with `claudeCliSupports(cliVersion, ...)`, exactly like
--strict-mcp-config, --setting-sources and --autocompact. Below the floor
the recorded prompt simply is not refreshed, which is the old behaviour.

The "CLI supports it" test also now calls `instance.snapshot()` first, so
the version floor is what admits the flag; without it the driver saw a null
version and would have pushed the flag for any CLI, passing for the wrong
reason.

**The room dedup compared the wrong spelling.** Requests and results reach
the transcript inside a JSON envelope (roomHandoffReport), so anything with
a newline appears escaped there. `roomContext.includes(child.result)` could
never match a multi-line result, so the brief was re-appended on top of a
transcript that already carried it — the exact duplication this check exists
to prevent. It now compares both spellings, and the fixture result is
multi-line so the case is actually covered.

- floor dropped to 0 → the "old CLI" test fails (flag pushed when it must not be)
- dedup reverted to a raw compare → the brief duplicates (length 2, not 1)

fix(vps): share SSH connections from the app and start the VPS for unattended runs

A person running OpenMausBot on their own server with the Self-hosted VPS
computer reported two things: scheduled routines that never used the computer
they were told to run on, and take-control that was painfully slow. Both were
the app leaning on the person's setup.

Slowness: every VPS action is `docker -H ssh://alias …` and the live desktop
is an SSH port forward. Docker's SSH transport runs the first `ssh` on PATH
with the person's ~/.ssh/config, so without ControlMaster in that alias every
command paid a full handshake — on each preview frame and each click. The
guide asked for the block; nothing checked. The app now runs every VPS SSH
connection through its own ssh_config under the data directory, which
includes the person's file first (ssh keeps the first value it sees, so their
settings win) and fills in ControlMaster, ControlPersist, keepalives and a
connect timeout where the alias leaves them unset, plus an `ssh` shim docker
finds ahead of the real one that points at it. Windows OpenSSH has no
connection sharing, so nothing changes there.

Scheduling: on Auto, a turn only reused a running container and never started
one unless Start VPS automatically was on. A scheduled routine has nobody
present to choose Cloud, so after the container idled out every run went
without its computer or, worse, onto the host's own desktop. Unattended runs
now start the VPS, and when it cannot be reached they fail with a reason
instead of touching the host.

Pair a phone's native app with a self-hosted server (#1188)

* fix(pairing): let a self-hosted server pair the native phone apps

The iOS and Android companion apps POST /api/pair, a route only the
desktop's companion sidecar ever answered. A self-hosted server therefore
had nothing for a native phone to pair against: the app could reach the
server, pass its health probe, and then ask for a six-digit code the
server has no way to issue. The sidecar that mints those digits ships in
neither the npm package nor the Docker image, so on a headless box the
code that generates them is not on disk at all. Reported twice in one
night by people who assumed they had misconfigured something.

A pairing window now has two encodings of the same secret. The typed
12-character code is unchanged. Alongside it the server mints
`omb_pair_` plus 43 base64url characters, which is the shape the
companions' QR parser requires, and hands back an
`openmausbot://pair?address=…&token=…&name=…` invite. Either encoding
redeems the window, once, under the same expiry and the same per-source
lockout, and the phone ends up with an ordinary session: it appears in
`openmausbot sessions`, it is revocable, and it is scoped.

A credential is hashed exactly as presented. Normalizing it would be
actively unsafe, since normalizePairingCode folds 0 to O and 1 to I,
which destroys a base64url secret and maps distinct secrets onto one
digest. That trap has its own test.

`openmausbot pair` now renders the app-scheme QR when pairing an Android
phone and keeps the web link as text, so neither route is hidden. The
guided flow's Android option stops saying "web browser", and the line
telling people the link is not for the native scanner is gone, because
it no longer is.

feat(coordination): resume delegated returns with only what the session has not seen

When a coordinate_bots result returned to a Claude or Codex conversation,
the harness cleared the provider cursor, and the next turn replayed the
last 40 messages into a fresh session although that session was intact.
Engines that resume strictly (new adapter capability strictResume) now
keep the session and are sent the context messages it has not been handed.

- server/delta-context.ts records, per task and provider instance, what one
  native session was handed (TaskRecord.handedMessages): the messages an
  accepted turn put in front of it, and the history older than the replay
  it was started from. A turn resuming that session gets the rest above
  its own text, newest first within 12 messages / 4,000 bytes; teammate
  content is never deferred and no body is clipped.
- A turn is recorded once the provider acts on it: output, a tool, an ask,
  or a successful completion. Error text a provider client produces itself
  (RuntimeEvent.synthetic) does not count. No output counts for a message
  steered into a running turn: it is offered again, marked as possibly
  already seen, until a turn the provider acted on carried it.
- A session.started for another session clears the record. A session the
  driver says it rebuilt from recoveryText (session.started.rebuilt) is
  credited with exactly that replay; any other replacement with nothing.
- Whenever the record cannot say what the session holds, the turn replays
  exactly as before: no record, another session's record, one that no
  longer lines up with the branch or has grown past its bound, an engine
  switched in before the update arrived, or anything a resumed session
  cannot take on changed since it started — persona, soul, section context,
  and for Codex the model and an effort it is not sent again. A turn
  carrying an update from outside its session is rebuilt with that same
  replay if its session is gone (SendTurnInput.recoveryIsReplay), which
  personal Codex threads now accept as well. Claude keeps a record only on a
  CLI that can refresh a resumed session's system prompt
  (--system-prompt-snapshot); an older one keeps today's fresh session for
  every delegated return.
- Stop keeps its meaning: what the person sent into a stopped turn is not
  offered to the next one, and neither is a queued follow-up that a restart
  recovered with an unknown outcome.

A bot's VPS computer is the desktop inside its one managed container. The
turn setup claimed that container's lease exclusively for the whole turn,

continue automatically", and failed after the 30-minute ceiling (Arjav,

feat(team): a broken run reaches the Chief of Staff, who can retry it (#1352)

* feat(team): a broken run reaches the Chief of Staff, who can retry it

A failed, stalled or unstartable run, or a failed routine, left one chip in
the thread it died in and nothing anywhere else. The person found it hours
later, from a phone, by opening the desktop and reading every thread, then
retried by hand. The pipeline sat still until they did.

The team already has a role for this. When a run breaks on a bot whose
section has a Chief of Staff (or that a Chief may coordinate), the incident
becomes a turn of the Chief's in its "Team incidents" thread: a chip naming
what broke, linked to the thread, and a report — who, which thread, what
the run said when it stopped, the last request and reply there, what to
do — marked as not from the person, quoted text as data. The Chief then
calls retry_thread (new, Chief-only: resumes the thread where it stopped
with a line saying who asked and why), delegate_bot with a corrected
brief, or says plainly that only the person can fix it.

Bounded: two retries per thread, then the report says stop; five incidents
an hour mutes the thread. A Chief's own failures and a section without a
Chief notify the person ("Ada hit a problem"). A thread another bot opened
and watches raises no incident — its delegator is woken already. A run the
person stopped is not an incident.

fix(computers): give every engine a provider-safe desktop tools/list (#1390)

v0.1.83 let Windows mount "This computer" (#1347), so every engine on
Windows began receiving the bundled cua-driver 0.22.1 tool list. Its
browser_prepare inputSchema has a root anyOf whose branches carry no
type: "object". Engines hand that schema to their model provider as-is,
and strict providers (OpenAI, xAI, Bedrock, Kimi) refuse it, failing the
whole turn: "tool parameter root must be an object type (root schema is

simply where the desktop newly reached those engines.

bridge now rewrites the answer to a tools/list into a plain object root:
root declarations stay authoritative, branch-only properties are kept,
allOf requirements are hoisted, and only requirements every anyOf/oneOf
choice shares stay required. Schemas that are already safe, tool
results, and every other frame pass through byte-for-byte. The driver
still validates each call against its own schema; upstream made the

The elapsed readout beside the Thinking label re-anchored to Date.now() whenever the selected thread changed, so switching between a bot's threads mid-turn showed 0:00 and counted from the switch instead of the turn's start. The client never knew the real start: busy is a bare boolean.

setTaskActivity now stamps turnStartedAt on a task's idle-to-busy transition and clears it on settle, mirroring busy/activity: runtime-only, reset on load, stripped from bots.json, and serialized through wireTask. ChatView anchors the timer to the stamped start (Date.now() stays as the fallback for servers without the field), so the count is truthful on every thread, including turns started by delegations and routines.

Turn start means first busy transition, so an approval parked on waiting-on-you keeps the original anchor; re-approval does not restart the clock.

Groups never showed the readout at all: their turns run on the group's busy slot, not on a member's task, so there was no stamp to count from. patchGroup now stamps turnStartedAt on every transition into a busy speaker and clears it when the group goes idle — the group-side twin of a task's stamp: runtime-only, reset on load, stripped from groups.json, and carried to clients through publicGroupState. GroupView anchors TurnPresence to it, so the working member's readout appears and resumes correctly after a switch to a 1:1 thread and back.

The thread behavior is pinned end-to-end by scripts/testing/thinking-timer-ui.e2e.test.ts: the fake engine holds a turn open in hang mode, a second thread is created through the same POST the sidebar's New-thread control dispatches, and the test switches threads mid-turn to require the readout to resume from the stamped start rather than the moment of re-selection. A second test in the same file covers the group leg: a one-member group created through the same POST /api/groups the sidebar's group creation dispatches (with setup completed, so the composer is live at once), a message routed to the default responder, and the group's claim of its speaker — the busyBotId transition the stamp rides on — must appear in the readout and resume from the same stamp after a switch away. The store invariant is unit-pinned in server/independent-task-store.test.ts: patches that never touch the speaker leave the stamp alone, re-claiming the same member does not move it, a different speaker restarts the count, and neither the speaker nor the stamp survives persistence or a reload. fix(approvals): let Full access stop the asking on OpenAI-compatible engines (#1401)

A user on Windows reported a Full-access Chief of Staff producing a
file-change card every couple of minutes, with only "Allow once" — no
blanket — across Grok 4.6, Muse 1.3 and Deepseek 4.1, and an "Always
allowed" panel that was empty and greyed out no matter which bot or model
they picked.

It reproduces, and it was not a misconfiguration. Those models all run on the
shared chat-completions runtime (driver kinds `openai-compat`, `grok` and
`minimax` — note `grok` the API driver is not `grokAgent` the CLI). For that
family, every route to "stop asking" was closed:

- `supportsApprovalMode(kind, "full")` was false, so the picker filtered Full
  out and it could not be granted to the bot at all;
- `delegationInheritsFullAccess` requires the recipient's engine to implement
  Full, so a Chief's grant could not reach it either;
- `hasNativeAutoReview` is false, so Auto behaves like Ask;
- the card is emitted with `allowSession: false`, and `createChatToolApproval`
  has no "always" concept at all — `answer()` only ever returns allowed-once
  or rejected;
- `allowKey`, which is what fills the "Always allowed" list, is set only in
  peer-approval.ts for bot-to-bot contact, so a file or command card can never
  add to that list.

The net effect was that a bot on any OpenAI-compatible engine had no setting,
anywhere, that would stop it asking before every single tool call.

Full access is defined in auto-approve.ts as "the person's explicit,
separately confirmed grant to answer every prompt". This family has no
provider reviewer to hand that grant to, so the runtime now honours it
itself: under Full the tool gate is bypassed rather than opening a card, and
the three driver kinds are added to the Full list so the level can be chosen
and can be inherited from a Chief. Auto is untouched — still no native
reviewer, still behaves like Ask.

Verified: both halves mutation-checked (reverting the runtime bypass fails
the no-card test; reverting the list fails the three capability tests), with
the Ask case asserted alongside so the Full case cannot pass vacuously — the
first version of that test raised no card in either mode because the tool was
never registered, which the Ask assertion caught.

fix(docker): copy the prepare hook before install so the image builds again (#1399)

releases and the platform installers were unaffected — only the container

fix(openai-chat): parse the leftover buffer on stream EOF (#1377)

* test(openai-chat): parse the SSE tail after an unterminated final frame

* fix(openai-chat): parse the leftover buffer on stream EOF

The SSE reader only parsed complete newline-terminated data: lines.
On EOF it flushed the decoder into the buffer but never ran that
leftover text through the same line parser, so a final
finish_reason/usage frame that arrives as the last bytes before the
socket closes (no trailing newline, no [DONE]) was silently dropped:
either the turn threw "Stream ended before completion", or, if an
earlier frame had already set finishReason, it returned with usage
still null.

Extract the per-line handling into consumeDataLine() and call it once
more on EOF with the leftover buffer, mirroring what the main loop
already does per line.

* fix(openai-chat): treat a stream cut mid-frame as an end, not a malformed frame

The EOF flush this PR adds also ran the malformed-frame path on a truncated
tail, which turned a clean stop into a hard failure. `delta-context.e2e`
caught it on Windows:

    offers the results again when the person stops the return turn before the
    provider acts on it — AssertionError: expected 'failed' to be 'settled'

When a person stops a turn (or a connection drops) the socket closes with a
partial frame in the buffer. On main that leftover never entered the parse
path at all — the `indexOf("\n")` loop cannot fire for it — so the turn
settled. With the flush it is parsed, JSON.parse throws, `malformedFrame` is
set, and `calls.finish()` throws "provider stream contained a malformed
completion frame".

An incomplete frame at EOF is expected; only a properly newline-terminated
frame that will not parse means the provider sent something bad. So the flush
stays and passes `atEof`, which suppresses only that flag.

Adds the truncated-tail test that branch never had: a complete
finish_reason frame followed by a cut-off one must settle ok. Mutation-checked
— dropping the `atEof` guard fails it.

fix(files): open a bot's link to a Windows path written with backslashes (#1380)

A bot on Windows links a file the way the OS spells it:
[Report](C:\Users\me\.openmausbot\workspaces\bot\report.md). Two things
broke that link.

- Rendering to HTML percent-encodes a destination's backslashes, so
  chatUrlTransform received C:%5CUsers%5C... . That no longer matched the
  drive-path pattern, fell through to the default protocol allow-list and
  came back empty: the link rendered as <a href=""> and a linked image as
  "Image unavailable". The transform now restores the separators before
  deciding; every other escape still reaches the server's single decode.
  A backslash image path also no longer becomes its display name.
- Markdown reads "\." as an escaped ".", so the destination parsed as
  C:\Users\me.openmausbot\... on both sides. The server authorized that
  collapsed path and then could not find it, and the attachment chip asked
  for it. A shared mdast extension keeps a backslash before punctuation in
  a link, image or definition destination that starts with a drive letter;
  "\\", "\(", "\)", "\<" and "\>" still escape. The server's authorization
  and image lookup, the message gallery, and the chat renderer all parse
  with it, so the path the client sends is the path the server grants.

fix(browser): a timed-out browser no longer wedges its session for good (#1501)

Field report (Kevin Ehling, macOS 27, cua-driver 0.22.1): a fill mid-MFA
failed with "Browser request timed out; restart the browser before taking
control", and from then on every call on that session — open, snapshot, close
all — answered "A browser action was interrupted. Restart this browser before
continuing." It survived restarting the app, deleting and recreating the
browser in Settings, and toggling the conversation's computer selection to
remount the tools. A teammate bot could not clear it either, since sessions
are lease-scoped per conversation.

`gate.uncertain` means a command the app already accepted might still be
executing inside the browser, so nothing else may touch it until a close
proves otherwise. A request timeout sets it — but the same timeout also stops
the transport, and stopping a client SIGKILLs the child tree and removes
itself from `clients`. The proof the latch waits for is therefore already in
hand, and holding it afterwards is what wedges the session: every agent tool
call passes through `withAgentAction`, so the tools that would recover it are
refused by the very state they would clear, and none of reconnecting,
recreating the browser, or remounting the tools closes the session. The only
way out was a person taking control in the browser panel and restarting it.

So uncertainty that came from losing the transport now resolves itself once
the client is gone. Uncertainty a human left behind — an interrupted human
command, an abandoned pressed key — still requires the explicit recovery it
always did: there the browser is alive and may act again. That distinction is
the new `lostTransport` flag; without it the fix would quietly delete a
safety property, which the two existing gate tests catch.

Mutation-checked both ways: dropping the call re-wedges the session and fails
the new timeout test; widening it to ignore `lostTransport` fails the two
human-input tests.

fix(desktop): hydrate and switch threads by page (#1527)

* fix(desktop): hydrate and switch threads by page

Two instances paired over a tunnel never got past "Connecting to the bot
server…": the companion has to buffer a JSON response whole to redact it
(MAX_JSON_BODY_BYTES = 32 MB), and `/api/bots` answers with every message of
every thread — 42 MB on the room this was found on, so the proxy replied 502
and loadAll() retried forever.

The parameters have been there for a while; this client never used them.
What moved is the weight of a message: since toolDetailPreview (2ef52bee,
v0.1.77) an activity row carries tool.input and tool.output, and that room's
activity went from 0.24-1.66 MB/day to 3.6-5.0 MB/day.

Hydration, the settings reconciles and a thread switch now ask for a bounded
page, and the "Show earlier" pill continues into the server once the held
page is mounted: it fetches through /api/threads/:id/messages?before= and
prepends, reusing the height capture that already keeps the viewport still.

Both switch endpoints learn ?messages=n for that. "0" keeps its meaning —
settings only, no messages key — and no parameter still answers with the
whole transcript, so no existing client changes behaviour. The parameter is
parsed before the switch, or a rejected value would leave the thread moved.

Transport only: nothing is stored, trimmed or redacted differently.

* fix(desktop): bound the switch frame, and validate before switching

Review follow-ups.

pageSize is parsed before store.switchTask / store.switchGroupTask, so a
value the server refuses can no longer move the selected thread on its way
to a 400. The test now parks the channel on its other thread first, which
the previous one did not: it asked for the thread that was already active,
so it would have passed either way.

The switch frame is bounded too. Both handlers built the whole transcript
with botWithThread / groupWithThread and broadcast it before answering with
a bounded page, which sent the history this endpoint exists not to send —
and overwrote the bounded snapshot every other client holds. The frame now
carries one default page with hasMore; only the unparameterised HTTP branch
materialises a full transcript, and an HTTP+SSE regression holds the frame
under a page on a 60-message room.

The transcript's captured scroll height now carries the thread it was taken
in. A switch between the capture and the commit would otherwise shift the
new thread's viewport by the old one's growth; the capture is dropped
instead, and the switch itself runs the effect that drops it.

* fix(desktop): fence a scrollback page against the transcript it asked about

A page asked for with `before=<oldest held id>` describes the transcript as
it stood when the pill was clicked. An edit, a branch switch or a thread swap
while it is on the wire leaves that answer describing a transcript this
client no longer holds, and prepending it reintroduces rows from the branch
that was left behind — the id dedupe cannot catch that, because those rows
are exactly the ones the client does not hold.

Each thread now carries a generation, bumped when its transcript is replaced
or its visible branch moves: a thread frame, a branch switch, a task switch,
and a room payload that carries a transcript. The request records the value
it asked under and the reducer drops a page whose generation has moved on,
clearing the loading flag so the pill does not stay spinning.

Ordinary appends deliberately do not bump it: a page must still land over
messages that arrived while it was on the wire, which is the common case.

refactor(server): add a route table seam so new routes land as modules (#1618)

server/index.ts is 18,847 lines and handleRequest is one 7,354-line chain
of about 225 route `if`s. Two thirds of recent commits touch that handler,
so every new HTTP surface conflicts with every other one. The builds that
come next (channels, maus routes, feed, repo API) add far more new surface
than they edit, so give them somewhere else to put it before they start.

- server/harness/http.ts: `json` and `readBody` moved verbatim out of
  index.ts and imported back. They close over no module state, so route
  modules can import them directly.
- server/routes/table.ts: `PASS`, `RouteContext` (req, res, url, path,
  method, the resolved RequestAuth, json, readBody), `RouteHandler`, an
  empty `ROUTES`, and `dispatchRoutes`.
- handleRequest runs the table once, right after the auth gate and the
  maintenance request counter and before the first inline route, inside the
  existing try so thrown {status} errors and the finally still apply. A
  handler that answered but returned PASS by mistake still ends the request
  (headersSent / writableEnded), so nothing can run twice. With ROUTES empty
  this is a no-op.
- The two new imports sit last in index.ts so a route module that pulls in
  other server modules cannot reorder today's module start-up.
- scripts/testing/verification-docs.test.ts treats index.ts plus the
  non-test modules in server/routes as the route registry, so it keeps
  working once a documented route lives in a module.
- server/routes/README.md states the rule: new routes are modules with
  explicit dependencies registered in ROUTES, not new `if`s in index.ts.

Deliberately not here: no existing route block moves, no `live` cells, no
shared getter context, no markers or checker. Those belong to the later
extraction work and only when it starts.

fix(chat): keep who sent a message when it is queued or steered (#1621)

On a shared or paired workspace a person's message carries `sender`, the
name resolved from their own session, so the transcript and the room
prompt say who spoke. That only held when the turn started at once. If
the bot or room was busy and the words were queued, waited for a free
thread slot, were steered from the queue into the running turn, or were
recovered after a restart, the line was appended without `sender` and
read as the desktop owner's profile name instead: bots addressed the
wrong person and the room transcript mislabelled the speaker.

The sender now rides the queue item (1:1 and room), is written into the
durable `chat_followups` payload, and is put back on the user message at
every place a queued line reaches the transcript: the 1:1 drain, the
room drain and its could-not-start fallback, both queue-to-steer
endpoints, and the restart recovery of a claimed dispatch. Pressing
Steer moves the words; it does not re-author them, so the stored sender
is used rather than whoever pressed it.

The payload field is optional. Rows written by an older build have no
sender and still load, drain and recover exactly as before.

`shared/wire.ts` gains one named type, `ResolvedSender` ({ name }), used
in place of the inline shape. No new fields, nothing is read from a
request body, and who may set it is unchanged: attribution only, never
authority.

test(server): poll delegation-suite states that were read too early (#1626)

Seven spots in the delegation e2e suites asserted immediately after a
condition that only becomes true once an async transition finishes, so a
loaded CI runner turned correct behavior into flakes (PRs 1576, 1615,
1507, 1228). Each now waits for the settled value, following the
expect.poll(..., { timeout }) shape from #1613:

- direct-coordination "queues a recipient at capacity": the Chief's
  {busy, waitingForTeammates} settles only after its dispatch turn ends;
  poll it for 15s instead of reading once.
- direct-coordination "starts independent work immediately": give the
  waiting-for-teammates poll 30s under load, and poll the final
  {busy: false, waitingForTeammates: false} rather than reading once.
- thread-aware "within capacity": a handoff within capacity can be
  dispatched at any moment after it is accepted, so its dump file may
  exist while the ledger snapshot still says queued. Require the dump to
  be absent only for threads beyond the admitted capacity, which are
  guaranteed to stay queued while the source turn is held.
- independent-threads-api "queues coordinated work behind a peer's
  approval": poll the handoff ledger for "queued" and "completed"
  instead of asserting immediately.
- routine-delegation "does not revive a cancelled routine": poll the
  terminal runState instead of reading it right after the wait returns.
- delta-context "replacement session ... rebuild could not replay": a
  send was steered when the previous turn had not settled; wait for the
  previous reply's turnTerminal marker before each send.
- codex-device-auth: the flow can report phase "succeeded" before the
  code is cleared; poll the full terminal shape in one assertion.

fix(server): keep pair conversations identity-stable across sender recreation (#1687)

A sender deleted and recreated under the same name never matched its
predecessor's pair row: resolvePairConversation filtered by opener id
only, so the recreated bot minted a second live kind:"pair" row while
the old one dangled live forever — split history, and one dead
duplicate per recipient that no live bot could reuse or close.

Match rows by sender identity instead: the opener's id while that bot
lives, else the one live bot the stamp's name still points at. A name
two live bots share inherits nothing — ambiguity never merges two
bots' histories. An inherited row is rebound to the live id on first
reuse (the hour it was opened stays), so the name fallback is needed
only once and a later namesake cannot claim the row.

A load-time sweep next to repairThreadUpdatedAts enforces the
invariant on data servers minted before this fix: at most one live
pair row per (recipient, sender identity). It keeps the row the
resolver favors and demotes the rest to closed plain threads — kind
cleared, closedBy stamped, history kept, never deleted, never
re-adopted.

Both stop() closures kill the CLI, so finalizeClose found an unsettled

fix(recall): a day named as session_search's until is the whole day (#1510)

`since` and `until` both went through parseSince, which reads a day name
or a bare date as that day's FIRST instant. So `until: "2026-09-16"` cut
the window off at 00:00:00.000 that morning, and the obvious way to ask
what happened on one day —

  session_search {"since": "today", "until": "today"}

spans no time at all and answers "nothing", with no hint that the window
rather than the history was empty.

Close the window on the last instant instead, for the three forms that
name a day (today, yesterday, YYYY-MM-DD). A span like "24h", an epoch,
and a date with a clock time still mean the instant they name, so every
other caller is unchanged.

fix(chat): show an edited message immediately on every platform

Editing a sent message kept the old question and its old answer on
screen until the new reply finished. The server forked the conversation
at once, but only announced the new message. Every client adopts a new
message as the visible branch only when it follows the message already
shown, and a fork is a sibling of the edited message, so the new branch
stayed hidden until a later snapshot.

  client's sendId on the fork; a retried edit with the same sendId
  returns the existing fork instead of forking and rerunning again.

  that hides the old answer, reconciles onto the server fork by sendId,
  and restores the old branch if the request fails.
- iOS + Android: a pending-edit stand-in replaces the message and hides
  the old answer while the request runs, and the fork in the response is
  adopted without ever hiding a reply that already arrived.
