fix(server): end the turn when its lazy computer claim rejects

Issue #1369, a follow-up to the lazy claim in #1368. A rejected lazy claim kept its slot fail-closed but left the turn busy indefinitely behind a gate that could only refuse screen calls, and the patched Computer wait ended chip could read as a contradiction while later calls kept refusing.

startAutoVmClaim now calls an optional slot.onRejected hook once, after marking the slot failed. The lazy Local VM and VPS registrations use it to surface a terminal computer-unavailable error activity, raise the turn-failed buzz and incident under the same rules as a dispatch failure (person-started turns only), and end the turn. The hook is fenced to the dispatch generation and a still-busy thread, so a rejection landing after settle or under a newer generation can never touch the newer turn.

Refusal semantics stay fail-closed: the gate keeps refusing while the turn tears down, and the teardown revokes the bridge capability so no late screen call can fall through to held:false.

fix(usage): headline the tokens actually bought, not the thread re-read each turn

`input` from every engine INCLUDES the provider's cache reads, so summing it
per turn counts the same system prompt and conversation once per message. A
six-turn thread that cost $0.28 reported 248.3k tokens "used"; 177.4k of that
was one cached prefix counted six times. It reads as a bug to everyone who
sees it, and it is the number people reach for when judging what a bot costs.

`freshTokens` already existed for exactly this — its comment cites #527 — but
only ChatView used it. This adds `headlineTokens` (fresh where the engine
reported a cached share, the raw total where it did not, which is the only
honest answer without one) and moves the remaining five surfaces onto it.

Measured on a real six-turn Claude thread: 248.3k -> 70.9k, actual spend
$0.2843.

The window indicator is deliberately untouched. Cached tokens genuinely fill
the model's context window — caching is a price discount, not a space saving —
so "Context N of window" must keep counting them.

fix: latch a setup-time room stall before it can reach provider dispatch

The room stall watchdog is armed at claim, but the stall completion
handler only exists once the provider turn runs. A stall during setup
found no handler, and setup could keep going and dispatch a provider
turn the person had already been told was stopped. The setup paths
that re-check capability currency abort on their own, but the
pre-id quarantine wait (waitForClear) has no such check after it.

Register a setup latch before the watchdog is armed. At the dispatch
site, swap it for the real completion handler synchronously: if the
latch fired, finish the turn as stalled without dispatching. No
cancelled handshake is marked on that path because no provider turn
was launched and nothing needs quarantining; marking would only delay
the next turn behind the TTL. The finally unregisters the latch on
every other exit.

The e2e parks a room turn in the quarantine wait, stalls it there, and
proves all three requested outcomes: no dispatch after the stall, the
claim released, and a later turn on the same room running. On the
unpatched code the same test fails by dispatching after the stall.

fix(queue): queue 1:1 messages behind a room turn

A person's direct message arriving while the bot ran a room turn
bounced with 409 thread_busy: startOrQueueDirectMessage's queue
condition covered capacity, an occupied thread, and coordination
parking, but not the room mutex. Add activeGroupTurnForBot to the
condition, mirroring startOrQueueOpenedThread, so the words queue with
a new "group-turn" reason instead.

The group-turn operation can outlive the last member's turn.completed:
the central fold releases the speaker, but the queued message's one
drain shot fires while groupTurnOperations still holds the bot, and
nothing re-runs the drain once the operation leaves the map. Drain in
finishGroupTurnOperation as well -- the drain's own block check
re-reads activeGroupTurnForBot, so a replacement operation begun in
the interim still keeps its ground.

The composer names the real bound on its waiting chip, and the
parallel-threads settings help now says what the limit governs: a
bot's 1:1 threads, one room turn at a time per bot, and delegations
waiting for a free thread (en, zh-tw, uk).

* test(context): name the reply after a stopped return turn explicitly

The stopped return turn's fixture sometimes records a turn of its own:
when the platform kills its MCP child before the fixture process, the
fixture fails and appends its evidence before it dies. The next turn's
plan was chosen by that evidence count, so it could land on the stopped
turn's gated plan or on the next entry depending on teardown order, and
the test opened the stopped turn's gate before sending. Keep that gate
closed (the stopped turn can never answer), name the next reply

* feat(desktop): organization library channel in Electron main

Contract 60 W2-2 (§5.1-5.6, §5.8). With an Admin that advertises
capabilities.library, the session's library pointer triggers a fetch of the
catalog and every release it names (not Off, format 2 or lower), each checked
against its SHA-256 before it is written owner-only under
<data dir>/org-library/blobs. catalog.json and an OS-encrypted
company-library.bin record let the saved catalog reach the runtime at start
before any request. The catalog is relayed to the local runtime as
openmausbot:managed-library; its unsolicited managed-library-state snapshots
become debounced install reports (on change, once per start, retried on the
next sync after a failure).

fetchLibraryBytes allows only the fixed library routes, with their own caps
(catalog 256 KiB, release 4 MiB, report body 64 KiB); the session keeps its
512 KiB cap. Sign-out, expiry, revocation, and an Admin that drops the
capability relay library: null and forget the catalog and cached files;
installed copies stay. Without the capability, or without an organization
account, nothing changes.

feat(ios): support iOS 16 so older iPhones can install (#1826)

A user in Japan could not download MausBot. Nothing was wrong with the
listing: the app is available in all 175 territories, free and rated 4+. The
block was the deployment target. At iOS 17 the App Store hides the app from
every iPhone that cannot run 17 — the X, the 8, the 7 and the iPad 5th and 6th
generation all stop at 16 and can never move past it.

The target drops to 16.0. Nothing is removed on current phones: every iOS 17
API is still used where it exists, behind `#available`, and the fallbacks live
in one file rather than scattered through the views.

- `onValueChange` / `onValueChangePair` back-port `onChange`, including its
  `initial:` form; 32 call sites move over
- `EmptyStateView` stands in for `ContentUnavailableView` (13 sites)
- `feedback(_:trigger:)` back-ports `sensoryFeedback` with the generators it
  wraps
- shims for `scrollClipDisabled`, `defaultScrollAnchor`, `selectionDisabled`,
  the 16.4 sheet chrome, the `pulse` symbol effect and `onKeyPress`
- `MicrophonePermission.request()` picks `AVAudioApplication` on 17 and the
  session call below it

What genuinely cannot work below 17, stated rather than faked:

- Live Activities need 16.1/16.2, so the widget extension is pinned to 16.1
  and the coordinator sits behind `LiveActivityBridge`. Answering from the
  island is an interactive widget, 17 only; on 16.1 the activity says "Open
  MausBot to answer" instead of showing dead buttons.
- Sending a credential from the phone uses HPKE, which is 17. It now fails
  with a plain message pointing at the computer, instead of a crash.
- `.defaultSize` is dropped: it only suggested an opening iPad window size and
  `SceneBuilder` takes no availability check.
- The chat opened at the bottom via `defaultScrollAnchor`. On 16 the existing
  scroll-to-last handler runs with `initial: true`, so it still opens on the
  newest message.

All 515 iOS unit tests pass. Built for device at 16.0; the widget extension
reports 16.1 and the share extension 16.0.

Restore the pi prompt split, re-anchoring on compaction (#1776)

* Keep Codex developer slot stable across volatile prompt changes

Only the stable half of the system prompt belongs in the developer slot:
it survives compaction unchanged, and any change to it invalidates the
provider cached prefix. The volatile half (memory, mentions, outstanding
teammate work) now rides the user input of the turn that changed it as a
labelled context block, matching the systemStable/systemVolatile contract
the Claude driver already implements. Ordinary roster or memory churn no
longer appends a second developer copy of the prompt to history or
re-uploads the conversation prefix.

Receipts in ~/.openmausbot/codex-instructions gain a volatile digest;
legacy bare-hex receipts parse as instructions-only and re-deliver once.

* Log prompt bytes by stable/volatile split in the usage ledger

Settled turns now record how many prompt bytes rode the cacheable prefix
versus the volatile half that legitimately changes, next to the token
usage they already book. This is the measurement the token-efficiency
work needs: it shows whether cache-layout changes actually shrink the
re-sent prefix, per task rather than per request.

* Move recent-work into the volatile prompt half

The recent-work block recomputes relative time labels ("2h ago") every
turn and its newest-first list changes as the bot works in other
threads, so its bytes differ on nearly every turn of an active bot even
when nothing else changed. Kept in the stable half, it invalidated the
stable digest each turn, which re-appended the full developer block and
flushed native history through inject_items, busting the provider prefix
cache. It is pure data ("your own past notes, not instructions"), so
delivering it after the cache boundary in the turn that changed it loses
no instruction weight.

* Share the stable/volatile prompt split across drivers

Extract the note wording and composition codex shipped into server/drivers/prompt-split.ts, plus the durable receipt store a driver whose native session survives a restart needs to avoid re-delivering a prompt the session already carries. codex.ts now builds its volatile note from the shared helpers; the strings are byte-identical, so no behaviour changes.

* Keep the chat drivers system message stable across volatile changes

grok, mistral, minimax and openai-compat rebuild their request from the stored transcript every turn, so a volatile section edit re-priced the whole cached prefix (tools, instructions, history). Put only the stable half in the system message and carry the volatile half inside the newest user message, which is fresh input on every request anyway. The note is delivered every turn, not on change: the stored transcript never contains the notes, so a digest-tracked note would leave the model without its memory on unchanged turns. Turns without the split keep the legacy single-block shape.

* Send the full ACP prompt once per native session

opencode, droid, grok, gemini, hermes, cursor, qwen and kimi share acp/core.ts, which inlined the entire system prompt into every session/prompt call - so the prompt accumulated once per turn in the agent session history and any volatile edit re-sent all of it. The establishing turn (or a stable-half change such as a soul edit) still carries the full prompt; later turns go through bare unless the volatile half changed, which then rides as the shared labelled note. Receipts are durable under the data dir, keyed by driver, thread and native session id, so a server restart that resumes a native session does not deliver a duplicate. Turns without the split (direct adapter calls) keep the legacy shape.

* Send the full pi prompt once per session

pi sessions persist their own history in a session file, so the system prompt previously accumulated there once per turn. Apply the shared stable/volatile split at the prompt seam: the full prompt rides only the turn that establishes - or re-instructs after a soul edit - the session, receipts are keyed by threadId+sessionFile and survive child restarts, and a failed handshake keeps the full block because the bare prompt would be the model's only context.

* Deliver mention context on every tagged turn

The mentions half of the volatile prompt describes the turn it rides, but its text only names the tagged bots, so two consecutive turns that tag the same bots produce an identical volatile digest and the second note was suppressed. Add SendTurnInput.mentionTurn, set when the turn tags teammates, and make every digest-based delivery path (codex receipts, claude session reuse, ACP, pi) deliver the note on tagged turns even when unchanged. The chat family already delivers every turn.

* Commit volatile receipts only after the provider accepts the turn

The volatile digest was persisted before turn/session submission, so a rejected turn/start or session/prompt left a receipt claiming context the model never received, and the retry went through bare. Codex now writes an instructions-only receipt at sync time and hands the driver a commitVolatile callback it calls after turn/start acknowledges; ACP writes its receipt only after session/prompt resolves; pi writes only after the prompt send leaves the process. A receipt whose volatile half is still pending parses the same as a legacy one and redelivers once.

* Redeliver the full pi prompt every turn

pi auto-compaction summarizes older user messages, and this driver delivers the prompt as the leading user message: a receipt-based split would let a compacted session keep running bare, without its standing instructions, while the receipt still claimed delivery. pi exposes no compaction signal on its RPC surface today, so revert to per-turn full-prompt delivery (the pre-split behavior) and keep the split for the families whose prompts survive compaction architecturally (codex developer slot, claude system prompt, chat system message) or whose agents keep full history (ACP). pi can adopt the split once its extension API (session_before_compact) can signal compaction to the harness.

* Restore the pi prompt split, re-anchoring on compaction

The revert's premise was wrong: pi's RPC surface does expose compaction.
AgentSessionEvent carries compaction_start/compaction_end for manual and
automatic compaction, and rpc-mode forwards every session event to stdout
(pi-mono packages/coding-agent/src/modes/rpc/rpc-mode.ts). So the split
returns, now with three correctness additions:

- compaction_start/compaction_end drop the session's prompt receipt the
  moment they arrive, so the next turn re-establishes the full prompt
  instead of running bare against a summarized history;
- the receipt commits only after pi accepts the prompt (its authoritative
  response - pi rejects prompts submitted while a compaction runs), and a
  compaction observed around the send suppresses the write;
- every eighth bare turn re-anchors the full prompt, bounding the damage
  from any history rewrite the events miss.

Per-turn full-prompt delivery cost ~13K tokens every turn and accumulated
one copy per turn in the session file; the split restores once-per-session
delivery with bounded re-establishment.

* fix(drivers): ACP re-anchor backstop; settle-guarded pi receipt write

- ACP sessions now pass ACP_PROMPT_RE_ANCHOR_TURNS = 8 to
  splitSessionPrompt, so an agent that compacts its own history without
  an event still gets the full standing instructions back within a
  bounded window, matching the pi backstop
- the pi prompt-acceptance rejection handler no longer emits a spurious
  runtime.error (and re-settles) once the turn already settled, and a
  failed receipt write no longer becomes an unhandled rejection

CodeRabbit follow-ups on #1776.

* test(vps): read the generated ssh config from a file, not /dev/stdin

spawnSync feeds the child's stdin through a socketpair, and Linux
refuses to reopen a socket through /dev/stdin (ENXIO), so the
quotes-spaces test failed on every ubuntu CI runner with:

  Can't open user config file /dev/stdin: No such device or address

macOS reopens its /dev/stdin fine and Windows skips the test, so
only Linux saw it. Write the generated config to a file whose name
keeps a space, so the quoting coverage is unchanged.

* fix(pi): settle only on the terminal agent_end so post-run compaction lands

turn_end no longer settles the turn: pi can schedule overflow-recovery compaction after a non-terminal agent_end (isTerminal: false), and killing the child at turn_end silenced those late events, leaving a stale prompt-split receipt until the 8-turn backstop. The driver now records the turn_end outcome, settles on agent_end with isTerminal !== false (the RPC contract terminal frame), keeps listening through non-terminal agent_end frames, accepts the auto_compaction_* event aliases, and falls back to a 60s grace settle for runtimes that never emit agent_end.

Regression-tested with a fake-pi compaction-recovery mode whose maintenance events land after the first agent_end; the test fails on the old code.

* fix(pi): honor upstream willRetry and agent_settled terminal markers

Upstream pi (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent, the package this driver installs) marks a non-terminal agent_end with willRetry: true and closes the run with agent_settled; the isTerminal field belongs to the omp fork dialect. Keep listening through willRetry: true frames, settle on agent_settled too, and cover both dialects with fake-pi recovery modes plus regression tests that fail on marker-unaware code.

* fix(pi): ignore turn_end frames that flush after the turn settled

A killed child can still deliver one buffered frame after settle; the abort path turn_end(cancelled) is the common one on Windows. Arming the agent_end grace timer there leaked it past a completed turn, which the ask fail-safe timer test catches as a leftover fake timer.

fix(acp): keep a turn alive while a quiet tool is running

The ACP prompt watchdog stops a turn when the agent sends nothing for
three minutes. It already waited for a person answering an approval, but
not for a tool the agent was running: a `sleep`, a quiet build or a test
run sends one in_progress update and then nothing until it finishes, so

feat(android): swipe right on a conversation to return Home (#1946)

* feat(android): swipe right on a conversation to return home

Android's system back gesture covers the screen edges, but only for
gesture navigation and only from the edge: three-button users have no
swipe, and the body of the conversation screen never answers one. This
extends the same meaning to the body of the screen through a reusable
horizontalBackSwipe modifier on the conversation's root surface, wired
to the exact exit chain the back pill and system back already take, so
the three affordances cannot disagree about what leaving means.

The detector claims a drag only when its horizontal slop arrives first
and nothing inside the screen has consumed: the transcript's vertical
scroll, the composer's selection, and any row control each win in the
main pass, and the modifier cancels the moment a child takes over. Net
travel decides at release, so a drag out and back is a change of mind,
and the system gesture insets are never claimed, leaving the platform's
edge behavior and predictive back exactly as the system defines them.

Verified by six Robolectric Compose tests, including one that mounts a
real navigator stack and session: a deliberate rightward drag pops the
conversation home and clears the chat draft exactly as back does, a
vertical swipe scrolls the transcript without waking the affordance,
and short, leftward, or reversed drags stay put. The unit-test JVM heap
is raised to 2g for the composition suites that render full frames.

fix(server): book Claude turns at their own cost, not the CLI's running total (#1891)

* fix(server): book a retained Claude process's turns at their own cost

Claude Code reports total_cost_usd as the running total of its process:
"cumulative across turns in streaming-input sessions — each result
carries the running total so far" (2.1.282), while `usage` is per turn.
The driver keeps one CLI process per thread across turns while the
spawn contract is unchanged, yet forwarded every result's total as
turn.completed.cost, which the harness books as that turn's own spend
(task totals, the usage ledger, the spend cap, digests). A retained
process's second turn was booked at the first two turns' total, its
third at the first three, and so on.

settle() now books the growth since the total the same process reported
for its previous turn. A process's first turn keeps its whole figure.
The share is taken where the turn settles, from the last total its
results reported, so it also holds for a turn that spans more than one
native result. A total that goes down is taken whole rather than booked
as a negative cost, and the subtraction is rounded to 1e-10 USD to drop
float noise.

The fake CLI now reports a running total as well (0.01 per result), the
way the real CLI does. A new driver test runs three turns on one
retained process and expects 0.01 each; before this change it got 0.01,
0.02 and 0.03.

* fix(server): book a resumed Claude session's first turn at its own cost

In the running server almost every Claude turn is a new CLI process: the
per-turn comms token in the MCP config changes the spawn contract, so the
next turn relaunches with --resume. On --resume the CLI (2.1.282)
restores the session's running cost, so that process's first
total_cost_usd, and its modelUsage, already count the earlier turns. The
driver booked the whole figure, so each turn was billed again for the
session so far: one real thread's ledger booked about $90 for roughly
$15 of work.

A result's modelUsage holds the session's running token counts per
model, while `usage` is the turn's own. The driver now keeps each
session's latest (total, modelUsage) states in
<data>/claude-cost-history.json (100 sessions, 8 states each), so the
record survives an app restart. On a process's first result it finds
the state the CLI restored: the earlier state that sits inside the new
counts and leaves exactly this turn's usage for one model. That is not
always the latest state; a process closed during a steered continuation
restored an older one. When no state fits exactly, because the CLI saved
work that never reported a result (an interrupted turn), the latest
state inside the new counts stands, so that work is booked once. With no
known state the turn keeps its whole figure, as before.

The fake CLI now reports modelUsage and, with FAKE_CLAUDE_COST_STATE,
restores a session's running cost on --resume. New tests cover the
helper against real frames, a resumed process with and without a driver
restart, and the usage ledger through the server, which booked 0.01 and
then 0.02 before this change.

* fix(server): measure a resumed Claude process from its first result with a cost

The first result after --resume decided the process's starting cost even
when it carried no total_cost_usd, as an API error result (529
overloaded) does. The start became unknown, so the next turn on that
process was booked at the whole running total again, restored turns
included. A result without a cost now decides nothing; the first one
with a cost is matched against the session's earlier states.

The fake CLI's FAKE_CLAUDE_RESUMED_API_ERROR plays the first turn of a
--resume launch as that error. The new test booked 0.02 for the turn
after it; it now books 0.01.

* fix(server): match a resumed Claude turn split over two models

restoredCostBase compared the turn's usage with each model's growth on
its own. A turn that used two models then matched no earlier state, and
the latest contained state won instead: with states A=2 ($0.01) and A=3
($0.02), a resume from the first plus one token on each of A and B
measured the turn from $0.02 and booked nothing. A state now also
matches when its growth summed over all models equals the turn's usage.
The one-model match stays: usage leaves out side calls on another model,
such as a Haiku title. Replaying real 2.1.282 logs gives the same figures
as before.

* fix(server): measure a resumed Claude turn from the latest known state

restoredCostBase took the highest total among the states that fit. A
resume that went back to an older state leaves later states with lower
totals (a real session went from 4.3538 to 4.2123), so the highest total
can be an older state from a lost branch. The start was then too high,
and a turn whose total fell below it was booked whole. Both the exact
match and the fallback now take the latest state in recorded order.
Replaying real 2.1.282 logs gives the same figures as before.

feat(decider): Jev decision model with room routing

Add a swappable decision-provider module (server/decider) modelled on the
TTS adapter: ask/choose/score/yesNo over a `jev` backend (TypeSafe
/v1/systemone, jev-latest, Bearer key) and an `off` backend, with a
baseUrl for a local Jev-compatible server later.

What it decides today: who answers an un-mentioned human message in a room
set to the new `auto` responder mode. One Choice over the room's active
bots (keyed by id, described by name/title/description) plus __everyone__,
with the last room lines as state. p >= 0.6 picks that bot (or everyone);
anything less sure falls back to the room's lead, else its first member.
@mentions, @everyone, goals and the other modes never ask. The decision is
started in startGroupTurn and awaited in its async round, so the append and
the send response stay synchronous; the title bot follows the pick. A
routed reply carries routedBy { provider: "jev", probability } and shows
"Picked by Jev · 94%".

It fails open: no key, switch off, job off, timeout (1.5 s for rooms),
network or HTTP errors (401/429/529/5xx) and malformed answers (a choice
that was not offered, non-numeric probabilities) all return
{ ok: false, reason } and the room behaves exactly as before. Answers are
validated strictly.

Settings gets a top-level "Decision model" item: one master switch (off
while no key is saved), the Jev key with Save and Test, and a "What it
decides" list (room routing, plus coming-soon rows). Saving a key turns the
switch and the room job on; a rejected key is not saved. The key follows
the TTS key path end to end: config section `decider`, OMB_JEV_API_KEY
env override (stripped from engine envs, redacted in diagnostics), the
desktop's encrypted credential store, an external-storage tombstone, and
booleans only in GET /api/config. Saving it never reloads the engine fleet.

Each call is logged to <data>/decider-log/YYYY-MM.ndjson (0600) with the
seam, choice key, pTop, margin, latency, tokens and a state hash; never the
message text or the key. The log is left out of workspace backups.

`auto` loads everywhere rooms are read: stored rooms, packages, team
backups and legacy team files; an unknown kind degrades to the first
member as lead. Package exports spell an Auto room as its lead so older
apps can still open them.

fix(desktop): recognise this computer's lease after a hostname change

The data-directory lease compared a leftover record's host with
os.hostname() before asking whether its process was alive. macOS renames
the host when it joins another network, so a lease left by a crash or
force-quit on one network looked like another machine's on the next: the
desktop refused to start ("still has a delegated server on another
machine", or "already owned by a process on another machine") until the
file was deleted by hand.

A record now counts as this computer's when it has the same hostname or
the same boot session id, which is random per boot and never shared
between computers; the existing dead-owner recovery then runs as before.
A record under another name from another boot cannot be told apart from
another computer's and still fails closed, but the message now says how
to recover when no other computer shares the folder. No new subprocess
calls or lease fields.

Fixes MOCA-270
